FILMEDIA 475: This course approaches the Russian and Soviet avant-gardes through three central themes: things, forms, and thinking. 'Things' speaks to such key concepts as dialectical materialism, nonobjective art, and faktura. 'Forms' encompasses the intricate paths of Russian Formalism as well as Constructivist design. 'Thinking' threads through things and forms as they were understood to shape subjectivities. We will consider many arts: literature and poetry, visual arts, fashion, architecture and film, placing the greatest emphasis on film. Our reading will be wide-ranging in terms of time and discipline. It will include, among others, avant-garde artists such as Kazimir Malevich and Sergei Eisenstein and their contemporaries Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Eikhenbaum. We will also read more contemporary art historians such as Christina Lodder, Yves-Alain Bois, John Bowlt, T. J. Clark, Christina Kaier, and Aglaya Glebova; film and literary scholars such as Jessica Merrill, Nariman Skakov, and Emma Widdis; and Russian historians such as Sheila Fitzpatrick, Terry Martin, and Yuri Slezkine. Films range from melodrama (Olga Preobrazhenskaya's 1927 The Peasant Women of Ryazan) to Dziga Vertov's documentaries and Eisenstein's Ivan the Terrible (1945 and 1958). We will also make time to look at archival materials in Special Collections.
FILMEDIA 481: Films and moving image works by contemporary filmmakers from Asia, including Hou Hsiao-hsien, Tsai Ming-liang, and Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Topics include explorations of national and local histories, aesthetics of slowness and duration, and crossings between the movie theater and the gallery.
FILMEDIA 490: In the 1950s, Truffaut proposed that the best cinema expressed the sensibility of the director. He, and critics who followed, even found "auteurs" (authors) in films from the "factory" of the Hollywood studios; including Howard Hawks. Critic Robin Wood and filmmaker Quentin Tarantino each cited Rio Bravo as the best film ever made, and Mulvey exempted him from the "male gaze." He marked westerns, comedies, gangster films, musicals, and scifi, specializing in groups under pressure, people defined by their jobs: the recurring issue is whether they're "good enough" to be part of the group, or the couple, or the world.
FILMEDIA 491: This seminar explores the visual legacy of civil unrest in the United States. Focusing on the 1965 Watts Rebellion, 1992 Los Angeles Riots, 2014 Ferguson Uprising, and 2020 George Floyd Uprisings students will closely examine photographs, television broadcasts, newspapers, magazines, and film and video representations of unrest. Additionally, students will visually analyze the works of artists who have responded to instances of police brutality and challenged the systemic racism, xenophobia, and anti-Black violence leading to and surrounding these events.
FILMEDIA 495: India is the world's largest producer of films, with Bollywood and other popular film cultures more recently being most visible on the festival and academic publishing circuit as well as university curricula. This seminar brings a rare focus instead to the various "art cinemas" of India, revisiting an extraordinary but neglected moment, extending from 1969 to the 1980s, when a constellation of alternative film practices emerged at the intersection of state interventions, oppositional politics, and a range of regional and transnational influences and exchanges. This upsurge in filmmaking outside mainstream cinema was dubbed the "Indian New Wave" or "parallel cinema." The goals of this graduate seminar include: Exploring the heterogeneous film cultures of the New Waves across multiple languages, categories of documentary and fiction, experimental and political cinema; Studying the relationship of the Indian New Waves to Third Cinema and other global art cinema traditions; Disrupting and expanding Eurocentric histories of art and political cinema; Examining the afterlives of the Indian New Waves through contemporary films and critical discourses on caste, gender, and sexuality; Cross-pollinating approaches that have traditionally been binarized across the art-popular cinema divide to foreground questions of dis/pleasure, cinephilia, stardom, labor networks, and the potential of gossip and anecdote as methodological approaches. For participants whose area of focus lies outside of South Asia, the seminar aims to discuss broader questions of cinema in relation to institutional networks in postcolonial contexts, state patronage and censorship, transnational influences and affiliations, infrastructures of canon formation, and new approaches to studying cinematic "new waves."
FILMEDIA 620: For Art History Ph.D. candidates. Prerequisite: consent of instructor.
FILMEDIA 660: For graduate students only. Approved independent research projects with individual faculty members.
FILMEDIA 680: CPT course required for international students completing degree.
